title: Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act of 2026
official_title: To amend the Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Act to reauthorize the provisions of such Act through fiscal year 2031, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Quigley (D-IL-5) with 103 cosponsors and cleared the House on July 22, 2026 before being placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 466). The measure extends an existing bipartisan program authored in 2021 without expanding federal spending authority beyond the existing $100M-per-year level, and adds oversight-tightening changes (adverse-event reporting, renewal-review safety and efficacy assessments) rather than new mandates that typically draw opposition. The main friction points are Senate calendar competition and any objections to the phase 2/3 combined-trial definition or the 5-year FDA action plan report burden — none large enough to defeat a rare-disease reauthorization with triple-digit House cosponsors.

referencedSources.label: Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Act (Public Law 117-79)

summary: This bill extends the 2021 Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Act — which authorizes HHS and FDA grants for expanded-access research on investigational drugs for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and other rare neurodegenerative diseases — through fiscal year 2031. It also tightens the underlying grants program by requiring safety and efficacy data on renewals, mandating prompt adverse-event reporting, expanding the "phase 3" definition to cover phase 2/3 combined trials, and requiring FDA to publish a new 5-year rare-neurodegenerative-disease action plan and follow-up report.
brief: Extends the ALS investigational-drug grant program and its $100M-per-year authorization through fiscal year 2031, and adds safety-reporting and renewal-review requirements.

top_lines.headline: What the Underlying Program Does
subs: HHS awards grants to small-business drug sponsors running expanded-access programs for people with ALS not eligible for clinical trials
FDA-NIH Public-Private Partnership advances rare neurodegenerative disease research
Authorized at $100M per year since fiscal year 2022

top_lines.headline: What This Bill Extends
subs: Extends the $100M-per-year authorization of appropriations through fiscal year 2031
Extends the grants program sunset from September 30, 2026 to September 30, 2031

top_lines.headline: New Grant-Program Guardrails
subs: Grant renewals must include HHS review of enrollment, safety, and any available efficacy data
Grantees must promptly report new and serious adverse events and unexpected safety information
"Phase 3" now includes phase 2/3 combined trials that begin enrollment within a Secretary-set timeframe

top_lines.headline: FDA Action Plan Refresh
subs: FDA must publish a new 5-year rare-neurodegenerative-disease action plan within 18 months of enactment
FDA must publish a report on actions taken within 5 years of enactment

items.main: Extends the underlying Act's authorization of appropriations — $100M per year — through fiscal year 2031 by striking "2026" and inserting "2031" in Section 7 of Public Law 117-79.
items.detail: Section 7 of the 2021 Act authorized $100M for each of fiscal years 2022 through 2026 to carry out the whole Act. This bill's Section 2(a) resets the terminal fiscal year to 2031, continuing the same $100M-per-year authorization ceiling for five more fiscal years without raising the annual amount.

items.main: Extends the sunset on the ALS investigational-drug grants program from September 30, 2026 to September 30, 2031 by amending Section 2(f) of the 2021 Act (21 U.S.C. 360ee note).
items.detail: Under the 2021 Act, HHS may not award new grants under the Section 2 expanded-access research program on or after September 30, 2026. This bill's Section 2(b) strikes "2026" and inserts "2031" in that sunset clause, letting the Secretary continue awarding grants for another five fiscal years.

items.main: Requires HHS to request and assess enrollment, safety, and any available efficacy data on the investigational drug when reviewing grant-renewal applications under the ALS research program.
items.detail: The 2021 Act's Section 2 authorizes grants to participating entities using data from expanded access to investigational drugs for ALS. This bill adds a new paragraph (4) to Section 2(b) directing that, on renewals, the Secretary shall request from the manufacturer or sponsor — and assess — enrollment, safety, and any available efficacy data relating to the drug's use in preventing, diagnosing, mitigating, treating, or curing ALS.

items.main: Requires grantees to promptly report new and serious adverse events and unexpected safety information from their phase 3 trial to the grant-making institution, on top of existing FDA safety-reporting rules.
items.detail: This adds paragraph (4) to Section 2(c) of the 2021 Act. Grantees must report to the grant-making institution in addition to complying with the safety reporting requirements under section 312.32 of title 21, Code of Federal Regulations (or any successor regulations).

items.main: Expands the definition of "phase 3" for participating clinical trials to include phase 2/3 combined trials that begin enrollment within a Secretary-determined timeframe.
items.detail: Under the 2021 Act, participating clinical trials had to be phase 3 trials conducted pursuant to an investigational new drug exemption under section 505(i) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. This bill's Section 3(c) adds paragraph (4) to Section 2(e) so that combined phase 2/3 trials also qualify as "phase 3" if they begin enrollment within a timeframe the Secretary sets in the grant's terms and conditions.

sections.label: Section 4 — FDA Rare Neurodegenerative Disease Action Plan

items.main: Renames the section heading and requires FDA to publish a new rare-neurodegenerative-disease action plan on the FDA website within 18 months of enactment, covering the following 5-year period.
items.detail: Section 4 of the 2021 Act (21 U.S.C. 360aa note) already directed the FDA Commissioner to publish a rare-neurodegenerative-disease action plan within 6 months of that Act's December 2021 enactment. This bill renames the section heading from "als and other rare neurodegenerative disease action plan" to "fda rare neurodegenerative disease action plan" and adds subsection (c)(1), requiring a new plan within 18 months of enactment of this Reauthorization Act that describes actions FDA intends to take over the 5-year period following publication with respect to program enhancements, policy development, regulatory science initiatives, and other initiatives described in subsection (a).

items.main: Requires FDA to publish a follow-up report on the FDA website within 5 years of enactment describing actions taken under the new action plan and the extent to which it meets the requirements.
items.detail: Subsection (c)(2) sets a 5-year post-enactment deadline for the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to publish a report describing what FDA actually did under the action plan required by paragraph (1) and the extent to which that plan meets the paragraph (1) requirements. The bill sets no penalty or consequence if the plan or report is late or omits required elements.

underreported.summary: The bill expands "phase 3" for grant-eligibility purposes to include phase 2/3 combined trials, and lets the HHS Secretary set the enrollment-start timeframe through the grant's terms and conditions rather than in statute.
underreported.why_unreported: The section is captioned as "Clarifying Participating Clinical Trial Definition," but the operative effect is to broaden which drug-development stages qualify for the ALS grants program and to leave the enrollment-window boundary to Secretary discretion rather than a statutory number.

underreported.summary: The bill renames the underlying Section 4 heading from "ALS and other rare neurodegenerative disease action plan" to "FDA rare neurodegenerative disease action plan," dropping the explicit ALS reference from the section title.
underreported.why_unreported: The reauthorization is framed around ALS, but the retitled Section 4 shifts the framing of the FDA action plan from an ALS-anchored plan to a general rare-neurodegenerative-disease plan without changing the substantive scope.

gaps: The bill extends the underlying Act's $100M-per-year authorization through fiscal year 2031 but does not itself appropriate any money — the actual dollars still depend on annual appropriations.

The bill retitles Section 4 as an "FDA rare neurodegenerative disease action plan" but does not extend or reauthorize the Section 5 FDA Rare Neurodegenerative Disease Grant Program (21 U.S.C. 360ee-1) separately.

The bill requires grantees to promptly report serious adverse events to the grant-making institution but does not define "promptly," specify a maximum reporting window, or provide penalties for non-reporting beyond the existing 21 C.F.R. § 312.32 obligations.

The bill requires an FDA action plan and 5-year report on rare neurodegenerative diseases but does not require any consultation with patient organizations, ALS advocacy groups, or the public-private partnership established in Section 3 of the 2021 Act.

The reauthorization does not address the HHS Public-Private Partnership for Rare Neurodegenerative Diseases established in Section 3 of the 2021 Act — the Partnership continues under the extended Section 7 authorization but this bill adds no new requirements or metrics for it.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Quigley
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, several years ago, a Chicagoan named Brian Wallach came to my office and shared the fact that he was just diagnosed with ALS, a devastating disease that steals a person's ability to move or speak. The average life expectancy at the time with someone diagnosed with ALS was 2 to 5 years. When Brian came to visit us in Congress, that was the reality he was facing. He cofounded an organization called I AM ALS with his wife, Sandra Abrevaya. Sandra's life changed overnight, too when she became an ALS caretaker.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Calvert
featured_quotes.text: As a Co-Chair of the bipartisan ALS Caucus, I saw first-hand the effort to get that landmark legislation across the finish line was the result of the passion and detepnination of the ALS advocacy community. The passage of the ACT for ALS Act authorized key programs to expand access to new investigational drugs and grants for research of this terrible disease. Working with my Appropriations Committee colleagues, the ALS Caucus, and ALS advocates, we have been successful at making historic investments into these programs.
